outcome: M. Cocos posted a long-dormant 2015 preprint (arXiv:1504.04852) through a series of major revisions from March 2025 through December 2025 (v4-v12), now titled 'A Proof of Chern's Conjecture for Flat Affine Manifolds,' claiming a proof for the flat (torsion-free, holonomy in GL(n,R) acting affinely) sub-case; the claim has not been digested, published, or endorsed by any expert source found, and the live Wikipedia article and other surveys continue to describe the conjecture as open.

disputes.summary: The claimed proof (arXiv:1504.04852) has undergone at least nine major revisions in 2025 alone (v4 in March through v12 in December), consistent with the author repeatedly patching gaps or errors found (by referees, readers, or self-review) rather than the claim being accepted as-is. No published referee report, journal acceptance, or expert blog/forum digestion (MathOverflow, Terence Tao's blog, etc.) was found endorsing or refuting the current version. The AMS Fall 2025 Western Sectional talk describing it as 'A posible [sic] proof' (not 'a proof') is itself hedged language from the author's own abstract.

A separate 2016 claim of a general proof by Huitao Feng and Weiping Zhang was found to have a serious flaw and was retracted (their corrected result instead gives an Euler-number formula for flat vector bundles); a 2020 claimed proof by Jianquan Ge (arXiv:2002.03105) was also withdrawn after errors were found (a Hessian-representation error identified by Andrea Clini, followed by the author's own discovery of an error in commutation of limits). Both of these predate the 26 January 2024 frozen revision and are recorded as history, not as events in the window.

summary: The problem as stated in this bullet is Chern's conjecture in full generality: the Euler characteristic of a compact affine manifold vanishes. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 - present), the only substantive development is Mihail Cocos's arXiv:1504.04852, a paper originally posted in 2015 (v1-v3, pre-window) that lay dormant until being extensively revised starting 31 March 2025 (v4) through 6 December 2025 (v12), now claiming a proof of the conjecture restricted to closed FLAT affine manifolds (i.e., manifolds admitting a flat, torsion-free affine connection) via a deformation argument on the Euler form using Stokes' theorem and a holonomy rigidity theorem. This is a genuine case of the stated problem (flat affine manifolds are a well-studied and important sub-class of compact affine manifolds, explicitly discussed in the problem's own Wikipedia article as the setting of Chern's original 1955 conjecture and of prior partial results by Kostant-Sullivan, Klingler, Hirsch-Thurston, etc.), so it counts under the §3.1 scope rule if credible - not a variant. However, I could find no evidence that any expert has read through and endorsed this proof: no journal acceptance, no MathOverflow or Tao-blog discussion, no citation as an established result in the one related paper I found citing it (arXiv:2510.09648, 'Affine-Orthogonal Manifolds and Deformation to Levi-Civita Connections,' Oct 2025), which cites Cocos's Theorem 2.3 only as 'evidence for Chern's conjecture,' not as a completed proof. The paper's own AMS Fall 2025 abstract is hedged ('A posible proof'), and the pattern of nine major revisions across nine months in 2025 is consistent with an unsettled, still-being-patched argument rather than a verified result. The current live Wikipedia article (checked today) still states the conjecture 'remains an unsolved mathematical problem' with no mention of Cocos's claim at all. Given all this, I classify status as 'claimed' (a preprint that experts have not yet digested) rather than 'resolved' or even 'partial' with confidence, and resolution_direction as 'confirmed' since the claimed result -- if correct -- would prove the flat case as conjectured (no counterexample, no refutation). I found absolutely no mention of AI/ML involvement anywhere in Cocos's paper, the AMS abstract, or any secondary source discussing it, and no lab or system is credited by anyone; ai_role is 'none'. I did also verify the pre-window history recorded in Wikipedia (Feng-Zhang 2016 retraction, Ge 2020 withdrawal) to confirm neither creates an open_stale situation -- both predate the window and neither was ever accepted, so they don't affect the window's classification.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be classified as 'open' with no_change_found, on the theory that an unrefereed, still-being-revised preprint with no expert uptake represents essentially no change to what a careful encyclopedia entry would say (which is exactly what the live Wikipedia article does -- it doesn't mention Cocos at all). Under that reading the nine-revision pattern is noise, not signal. I chose 'claimed' instead because the instructions define 'claimed' precisely as this situation (a preprint or announcement that experts have not yet digested) and distinguish it from 'open' specifically so that live, contested claims are visible in the dataset rather than folded into silence. The alternative classification names the same underlying facts but treats the lack of digestion as disqualifying rather than as the defining feature of 'claimed'.
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance or a public expert review (MathOverflow answer, referee report, a survey citing it as an established theorem, or discussion on a mathematician's blog) of the Cocos proof's current version would settle whether this becomes 'resolved' (if endorsed) or reverts toward 'open'/'incident' (if a fatal flaw is found and the paper is withdrawn, as happened to the 2016 and 2020 predecessor claims).

corrections.why: The claim is not credible enough to be the event the status rests on. The record treats 'flat affine manifolds' as a sub-case, but an affine manifold is by definition one with a flat torsion-free connection, so this is the conjecture itself, not a restriction of it. A 2015 preprint dormant for a decade and then pushed through nine major revisions in nine months, presented by its own author at AMS as 'a posible proof', on a conjecture whose two previous claimed proofs (Feng-Zhang 2016, Ge 2020) were both withdrawn, is the pattern of a claim still being patched. The one paper that cites it treats it as evidence, not as a proof, and the live Wikipedia article does not mention it. The record's own competing_reading proposes `open`. Nothing else in the window qualifies. DEPARTURE FROM THE INSTRUCTIONS, STATED PLAINLY: DEEP_DIVE.md 6.1 codes any undigested preprint `claimed` and the agent followed that correctly. This correction applies a stricter rule: a claim with no expert uptake, from outside or at the margin of the field, on a problem whose resolution would be a landmark, is set aside like a withdrawn claim, and the furthest genuine event that remains sets the status. The claim stays in `outcome`, `event` and `summary` as evidence; if it is ever digested this should revert to `claimed` or `resolved`.
